title: Not for the reward (Avot 1:3)
hook: Antigonus: be like servants who serve without thought of a reward
tomorrow: Sit in the dust of the wise

segments.voice: Yesterday, three pillars: the world stands on learning, worship and deeds of loving-kindness. Your line was three legs to stand on. Today, Simon the Just's student speaks. Day two hundred thirty-six.

Gold stars. Points. Streaks. Badges. Employee of the month. The world runs on little rewards, and to be fair, they work. Plenty of people learned to read for a sticker. But watch what can happen when the reward stops. The kid who read for stickers stops reading. The volunteer who wanted to be thanked quits when nobody does. Long ago, a sage named Antigonus, from a town called Socho, looked at this and gave advice that's hard to hear.
screen: `GOLD STARS AND STREAKS.` → `WHEN THE REWARD STOPS.` → `ANTIGONUS OF SOCHO.`

segments.voice: Antigonus received the tradition from Simon the Just, the next link in the chain. His saying, in paraphrase: don't be like servants who serve their master in order to receive a reward. Be like servants who serve their master not in order to receive a reward. And let the awe of heaven be upon you. The word for reward here is peras. Some commentators say it means something small: a tip, a treat, a little bonus a master tosses to a servant. Antigonus isn't saying good deeds go unrewarded. He's saying don't make the tip the point. Do the right thing because it's right, and because of who you're serving. An old story shows how easily this can be misheard. Avot de-Rabbi Natan, an early companion to Avot, tells of two students of Antigonus, Zadok and Boethus. They heard, don't serve for a reward, and concluded: then there is no reward, no world to come. And, the story says, they broke away and founded their own sects. Historians doubt the story, but the warning is clear: a saying about motive can be twisted into a saying about emptiness. Later, the philosopher Maimonides made peace with the gold stars. A child, he wrote, is taught first with sweets, then with new clothes, then with coins, and later with honor. That's fine. That's how people start. The goal is to grow, slowly, toward serving out of love: for the one you serve, and for the good itself.
screen: `SERVE NOT FOR THE REWARD.` · `PERAS — A TIP, A TREAT.` · `TWO STUDENTS WHO MISHEARD.` · `FROM SWEETS TO LOVE.` · then, large: `NOT FOR THE PRIZE.`

segments.voice: Look over the good things you did this week and notice, honestly, which had a little tip attached: a thank-you you were waiting for, a like, a favor owed. That's human, so don't scold yourself. Then think of one thing you could do today where no tip is possible, where no one will know and no one will thank you.
Peras. A reward, a small tip: the word in Antigonus's warning not to serve like a servant who expects one, but with awe of heaven.
Your line: not for the prize. The sweets are only where it starts. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 236 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: SIT IN THE DUST OF THE WISE.`

howItsDone: The Talmud teaches that a person should keep doing the commandments even for other motives, because from that they come to do them lishmah, for their own sake.

fork.setup: you're a student of Antigonus. your teacher says: don't serve your master for the reward. what do you conclude?
options: then there is no reward at all.
do the right thing for its own sake, whatever comes.
serve only masters who don't pay.
fork.reveal: Antigonus meant: don't make the reward the point. an old story says two students, Zadok and Boethus, concluded there was no reward, and broke away.

original.note: Hebrew: in order to receive a reward. The motive Antigonus warns against (Avot 1:3).

trapdoor: what you thought: be a selfless servant.
what it means: do good for its own sake and for the one you serve, not for the tip.
what a scholar hears: Avot de-Rabbi Natan tells that Zadok and Boethus misread this saying and founded the Sadducees and Boethusians, a story historians doubt.

kindness that goes past what's owed

chat.says: Is it wrong to do good things just to get a reward?
options: It is how many start. But Antigonus says: don't make the reward the point.
Antigonus taught that good deeds never bring any reward at all.
Yes, and Maimonides said children should never get sweets for learning.
chat.meaning: Antigonus: don't serve for the peras, the tip. Maimonides says starting with sweets is fine; the goal is to grow toward serving out of love.

Antigonus.meaning: a sage who received the tradition from Simon the Just

Maimonides.meaning: a great medieval Jewish philosopher and legal scholar

Avot de-Rabbi Natan.meaning: an early companion book to Pirkei Avot

sources.ref: Maimonides, Commentary on the Mishnah, introduction to Sanhedrin 10 (Perek Chelek)

notes: Peras as a small gratuity (vs. a wage): a reading found in several commentators; confirm.
Zadok and Boethus story from Avot de-Rabbi Natan (A) 5; presented with the caveat that historians doubt it.
Maimonides' analogy of the child (sweets, coins, honor) from the introduction to Perek Chelek; confirm.
'Two thousand years ago' for Antigonus is approximate (c. 3rd–2nd century BCE).
